What you get in this pack
Everything one teacher or tutor needs to place a new student in 45–60 minutes, score reasoning on
one page per level, and report progress to parents with evidence.

pages

diagnostic

script for parents.
6 student
worksheets
One CEIW card for each of Levels 1–5, plus a reﬂection sheet for every level.
5 scoring
sheets
One per level, four bands (Emerging, Developing, Secure, Advanced) and 18 feedback codes.
40 scored
examples
The Calibration Exemplar Bank: eight examples per level, each with the band, the reasoning behind it and
the next move.

1. How this kit works
Jurassic English™ assesses how
a
student
reasons: can they take a position (Claim), support it from the text
(Evidence), explain what the evidence means (Interpretation), name the principle that links them (Warrant) and,
at the top level, say what the argument means for the wider world (Impact)? Together these are called CEIW.
Each level adds one move:
Level Ages
(typical) CEFR CEIW
moves
taught Sentence
frame
L1 Foundation 4–8 Pre-A1 →  A1 Claim "I think… because…"
L2 Development 8–10 A1 →  A2 Claim + Evidence "In the text, the
author writes that
___."
L3 Expansion 10–12 A2 →  B1 Claim + Evidence +
Interpretation
"This may suggest
that ___."
L4 Mastery 12–14 B1 →  B2 + Warrant "Underlying this is the
principle that ___."
L5 Advanced 14+ B2 →  C1 + Counter-warrant
and Impact
"An alternative
principle would hold
that ___. If accepted,
this argument has
implications for ___."
Every piece of work is scored in four bands: Emerging
·
Developing
·
Secure
·
Advanced. A student moves up
a level when they reach Secure
or
higher
on
every
required
move,
across
three
separate
pieces
of
work.

cycle: place the student (Section 2) →  teach and collect worksheets (Section 3) →  score with the sheets
(Section 4) →  report to parents (Section 5) →  check progress each term (Section 6) →  keep the evidence
(Section 7).

54Licensed for one teacher or tutor. © Jurassic English
4. Level 3 Exemplars — Developing Analyst (A2 / B1)
CEIW
Depth: Claim + Evidence + Interpretation. Modality: Multi-paragraph (typically two paragraphs); paired-
text response; spoken interpretation. Reminder: The most common failure at L3 is interpretation-as-
restatement. The examples below are calibrated to make this distinction visible.
Exemplar
3.1
—
Emerging
Field Content
Level 3 — Developing Analyst
CEFR band A2+
Rubric band Emerging
Text / prompt context Short story about a student, Lan, who ﬁnds her classmate's wallet
and quietly returns it, telling no one. Prompt: "What
does
this
story
suggest
about
Lan's
character?"
Student response sample "The story is about Lan. She ﬁnds a wallet. She returns it. She
does not tell anyone. This is the story."
CEIW annotation Claim: not formed. Evidence: present as plot summary.
Interpretation: missing.
Assessor comment The response is an accurate plot summary. There is no claim about
character and no interpretive move.
Why this band is accurate A Developing response would attempt a claim, even vague. This
response treats the prompt as a "retell" task.
Revision target Add a claim: "Lan
is
honest
and
humble." Then keep the events as
evidence and add a "this suggests" sentence.
DRE artifact type Paragraph; tagged "L3, Justify, M-C, M-I."
Teacher feedback code M-C, M-I
Exemplar
3.2
—
Emerging
Field Content
Level 3 — Developing Analyst
CEFR band A2+
Rubric band Emerging
Text / prompt context Article about students who organize a school garden to grow
vegetables for the cafeteria. Prompt: "What
does
the
article
suggest
about
the
value
of
student-led
projects?"
Student response sample "Student-led projects are good. The students grow vegetables. The
cafeteria uses them. Everyone is happy."
CEIW annotation Claim: present but vague ("good"). Evidence: cited at sentence
level. Interpretation: absent.
Assessor comment The claim is non-speciﬁc. Evidence is on-topic but unconnected to
a precise claim. No interpretation.
Why this band is accurate The claim is too generic, and there is no interpretive sentence. A
Developing response would attempt at least a vague interpretation.
Revision target Add: "This
may
suggest
that
students
learn
responsibility
when
they
take
care
of
something
real."
DRE artifact type Short paragraph; tagged "L3, Justify, M-I."
Teacher feedback code W-C, M-I

Exemplar
3.3
—
Developing
Field Content
Level 3 — Developing Analyst
CEFR band B1
Rubric band Developing
Text / prompt context Same Lan-and-the-wallet story. Prompt: "What
does
this
story
suggest
about
Lan's
character?"
Student response sample "The story suggests that Lan is honest. She ﬁnds a wallet on the
ﬂoor. She returns it to her classmate. She does not tell anyone.
This shows that she returned the wallet quietly."
CEIW annotation Claim: clear. Evidence: cited. Interpretation: present but is
restatement of the action.
Assessor comment The interpretation sentence ("This shows that she returned the
wallet quietly") repeats what the evidence already said. The
interpretive move is absent.
Why this band is accurate A Secure response would add meaning beyond the event: "This
may
suggest
that
Lan
values
honesty
more
than
recognition." This
response stops at description.
Revision target Replace the ﬁnal sentence with an inference about Lan's values,
not her actions.
DRE artifact type Paragraph; tagged "L3, Justify, I-R."
Teacher feedback code I-R
Exemplar
3.4
—
Developing
Field Content
Level 3 — Developing Analyst
CEFR band B1
Rubric band Developing
Text / prompt context Poem about birds migrating across a wide ocean and resting
brieﬂy on a small ship. Prompt: "What
does
the
poem
suggest
about
the
journey?"
Student response sample "The poem suggests the journey is hard. The birds ﬂy very far. They
are tired. They land on a ship. This means the birds need to rest."
CEIW annotation Claim: present. Evidence: cited. Interpretation: drifts into
restatement.
Assessor comment The ﬁnal sentence ("the birds need to rest") restates the event
("they land on a ship") rather than interpreting it.
Why this band is accurate The interpretation is paraphrased evidence, not added meaning.
The restatement pattern is the canonical L3 Developing failure.
Revision target Replace with: "This
may
suggest
that
even
small
kindnesses
—
a
ship
willing
to
wait
—
make
long
journeys
possible."
DRE artifact type Paragraph; tagged "L3, Justify, I-R."
Teacher feedback code I-R

56Licensed for one teacher or tutor. © Jurassic English
Exemplar
3.5
—
Secure
Field Content
Level 3 — Developing Analyst
CEFR band B1
Rubric band Secure
Text / prompt context Article about a town that decided to ban single-use plastic bags.
Prompt: "What
does
the
article
suggest
about
how
communities
change
their
habits?"
Student response sample "The article suggests that communities can change their habits
when small actions are visible. For example, the town bakery
started using paper bags ﬁrst. Other shops follow within a month.
This may suggest that change spreads when people see one
neighbor try something new. The article shows that the ﬁrst step
matters more than perfect rules."
CEIW annotation Claim: precise. Evidence: a speciﬁc sequence cited. Interpretation:
clear and distinct from the evidence.
Assessor comment The interpretation adds genuine meaning ("change spreads when
people see one neighbor try something new") that is not contained
in the cited event. Hedging ("may suggest") is appropriate at B1.
Why this band is accurate This hits L3 expectations cleanly. Not yet Advanced because the
response does not consider counter-examples or paired evidence.
Revision target Add: "However,
in
some
towns,
public
habits
change
only
when
rules
are
also
enforced." (introduces a qualifying counter-example,
L4 precursor.)
DRE artifact type Paragraph; tagged "L3, Publish, secure."
Teacher feedback code +CL, +EV, +I
Exemplar
3.6
—
Secure
Field Content
Level 3 — Developing Analyst
CEFR band B1
Rubric band Secure
Text / prompt context Short story about two friends, Ana and Mei, whose friendship is
broken by a misunderstanding and later mended through a written
letter. Prompt: "What
does
the
story
suggest
about
repair
after
conﬂict?"
Student response sample "The story suggests that written words can repair what spoken
words are damaged. Ana and Mei argue loudly in the schoolyard.
They do not speak for a week. Then Ana writes a letter to Mei and
explains carefully what she meant. Mei reads the letter twice. They
meet and laugh again. This may suggest that writing gives time to
think, while speaking can hurry our anger."
CEIW annotation Claim: precise. Evidence: three cited story moments.
Interpretation: distinct, principled, and properly hedged.
Assessor comment The ﬁnal sentence interprets why writing repaired what speech
broke — it adds meaning beyond the events.
Why this band is accurate Strong L3. Slightly below Advanced because there is no second
supporting interpretation or comparative move.
Revision target Compare a paired text on conﬂict resolution; or add a second
interpretation about the role of time.
DRE artifact type Paragraph; tagged "L3, Publish, secure."
Teacher feedback code +CL, +EV, +I
